title: Explain the static keyword (static variables, methods, blocks, nested classes) and why the entry point main is static.
shortTitle: What is the static keyword and why is main static?

s1_definition.profdef: The `static` keyword binds a member to the class itself rather than to any individual instance. A static variable is a single shared field that all instances see and that exists once per class. A static method belongs to the class and can be called without creating an object, but it cannot access instance state directly. A static initializer block runs once when the class is loaded, used to set up static state. A static nested class is associated with the outer class but does not hold a reference to an outer instance. The `main` method is static so the JVM can invoke it to start the program without first creating an instance of the class.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a static variable is like the single shared total of all deposits held at head office; every branch sees and updates the same one number. A static method is like a service you can call at head office directly, such as computing the standard fee, without needing to open a specific customer's account first. A static block is like the one-time setup head office does when it first opens for business each morning. The static main method is like the bank's front door that the regulator can walk through to start operations without anyone needing to first create a customer; the entry point must be reachable without an existing instance.
s1_definition.oneliner: `static` means it belongs to the class, not an instance — one copy shared by all, callable without an object, which is why `main` is static.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The `static` keyword binds a member to the class itself rather than to any individual instance. A static variable is a single shared field that all instances see and that exists once per class. A static method belongs to the class and can be called without creating an object, but it cannot access instance state directly. A static initializer block runs once when the class is loaded, used to set up static state. A static nested class is associated with the outer class but does not hold a reference to an outer instance. The `main` method is static so the JVM can invoke it to start the program without first creating an instance of the class.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a static variable is like the single shared total of all deposits held at head office; every branch sees and updates the same one number. A static method is like a service you can call at head office directly, such as computing the standard fee, without needing to open a specific customer's account first. A static block is like the one-time setup head office does when it first opens for business each morning. The static main method is like the bank's front door that the regulator can walk through to start operations without anyone needing to first create a customer; the entry point must be reachable without an existing instance.

**One line to remember:** `static` means it belongs to the class, not an instance — one copy shared by all, callable without an object, which is why `main` is static.

sections.s2_technical:
A static variable, also called a class variable, exists once per class regardless of how many instances you create. Every instance shares the same storage. This is ideal for things that are truly shared, like a counter of total transfers across the whole system, or a configuration constant. It lives in the method area or Metaspace and is initialized when the class is loaded.

A static method belongs to the class and is called on the class, such as `Math.max` or a utility `FeeCalculator.standardFee`. Because it is not tied to an instance, it has no `this` and cannot directly access instance fields or instance methods; it can only work with static state or with objects passed to it as parameters. Static methods are great for stateless utilities and factory methods.

A static initializer block is a block of code written as `static { ... }` that runs exactly once when the class is loaded and initialized, before any instance is created and before main runs if it is in the main class. It is used for complex one-time setup of static fields, such as loading a lookup table.

A static nested class is a class declared inside another class with the `static` modifier. Unlike an inner class, it does not hold an implicit reference to an enclosing instance, so it does not cause the outer object to be kept alive. It is used to logically group a helper type with its outer class, like a static `Builder`.

The `main` method is static for a fundamental reason: the JVM needs an entry point it can call before any objects exist. When you run `java com.bank.App`, the JVM loads the class and calls `main` directly on the class. If main were an instance method, the JVM would face a chicken-and-egg problem: it would need an instance to call main, but creating that instance is itself application logic the program has not started yet. Making main static breaks this cycle. A senior nuance is that static members are initialized lazily on first active use of the class and are tied to class loading, and that overusing static mutable state is an anti-pattern because it creates global shared state that is hard to test and dangerous under concurrency, which is why in banking we keep shared static state immutable or carefully synchronized.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank wants a single running count of how many transfers the whole system has processed since startup, shared across every service instance in the process. This is exactly what a static variable provides — one shared copy per class.

Problem 2 — The bank has a standard fee calculation that does not depend on any particular account and should be callable without creating an object. This is exactly what a static method provides.

Problem 3 — At startup, the bank must load a one-time table of branch codes before any transfer runs. This is exactly what a static initializer block does — runs once at class load.

Problem 4 — The program must start without anyone first creating an object, which is exactly why main is static, letting the JVM call it directly.

The code has a `TransferService` with a static counter and a static block, a static utility `FeeCalculator`, and a `StaticDemo` main class.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
static-keyword-demo/
├── src/
│   └── main/java/com/bank/statics/
│       └── StaticDemo.java   (main + Account + FeeCalculator + TransferService)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/statics/StaticDemo.java

# Run (JVM calls the static main directly, no instance created)
java -cp out com.bank.statics.StaticDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two transfers, 50000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001 and 10000 back, with a standard fee computed on 50000.

Step 1: The JVM loads the StaticDemo class and calls its static main directly. No StaticDemo object is ever created, which only works because main is static.

Step 2: When the TransferService class is first referenced, it is loaded, and its static block runs exactly once, loading the branch codes table and logging that it happened. This occurs before any TransferService instance exists.

Step 3: The static method FeeCalculator.standardFee is called on the class with 50000. Because it is static, no FeeCalculator object is needed. It returns a fee of 10 rupees.

Step 4: The first transfer runs. It debits SAV2001, credits CUR3001, and increments the shared static counter totalTransfers from 0 to 1.

Step 5: The second transfer runs similarly and increments the shared static counter from 1 to 2. Both transfers used the same single counter, demonstrating that static state is shared across all usage.

Step 6: The static getter reports the total as 2. The static branch codes table, loaded once in the static block, was used by both transfers without being reloaded.

```text
INFO: Static block: branch codes loaded once at class load
INFO: Standard fee on 50000 = Rs.10.00
INFO: Transfer 50000 SAV2001(MUM-001) -> CUR3001(MUM-002)
INFO: Transfer 10000 CUR3001(MUM-002) -> SAV2001(MUM-001)
INFO: Total transfers system-wide = 2
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  java com.bank.statics.StaticDemo
    │ JVM loads class, calls static main (NO instance)
    ▼
  First use of TransferService
    │ class loaded → static {} block runs ONCE → BRANCH_CODES filled
    ▼
  FeeCalculator.standardFee(50000)   (static method, no object)
    │ → Rs.10.00
    ▼
  transfer #1  → totalTransfers: 0 → 1   (shared static var)
  transfer #2  → totalTransfers: 1 → 2   (same shared var)
    ▼
  getTotalTransfers() → 2
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — static Members by Kind ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          TransferService              │
  │ ─────────────────────────────────────│
  │ - static totalTransfers: int          │  class-level shared state
  │ - static BRANCH_CODES: Map            │  loaded in static {}
  │ - repo: AccountRepository             │  instance field
  │ ─────────────────────────────────────│
  │ static {} block → runs once at load   │
  │ + transfer(...): void                 │  instance method (uses this)
  │ + static getTotalTransfers(): int     │  class method (no this)
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘

  Rules:
   static var    → one copy per class, shared by all instances
   static method → no 'this', cannot touch instance fields directly
   static block  → runs once at class load, before any instance
   static nested → no implicit outer reference (e.g. Builder)
   main static   → JVM calls it with NO instance (breaks chicken-egg)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The static keyword binds a member to the class itself rather than to any individual instance, and it applies to variables, methods, initializer blocks, and nested classes.

A static variable, or class variable, exists exactly once per class and is shared by every instance. I use it for things that are genuinely shared across the whole process, like a counter of total transfers. A static method belongs to the class and can be called without creating an object, which makes it ideal for stateless utilities like a fee calculator; because it has no this, it cannot directly touch instance state. A static initializer block runs exactly once when the class is loaded, which is the right place for one-time setup such as loading a lookup table of branch codes. A static nested class is grouped with its outer class but, unlike an inner class, holds no reference to an outer instance, which is why builders are usually static nested classes.

The main method is static for a very concrete reason. The JVM needs an entry point it can call before any objects exist. When I run the java command, the JVM loads the class and calls main directly on it. If main were an instance method, the JVM would need an instance to call it, but creating that instance is itself application logic that has not started yet, so it would be a chicken-and-egg problem. Making main static breaks that cycle, letting the program bootstrap cleanly.

In our banking service this all comes together naturally. The shared total-transfers counter is a static variable, the standard fee calculation is a static utility method, and the branch-code table is loaded once in a static block at class load. The one caution I always add is that overusing static mutable state is an anti-pattern, because it is effectively global state that is hard to test and dangerous under concurrency, so I keep shared static state either immutable or carefully synchronized, which matters a great deal in a multi-threaded banking system.

---

keyPoints: static: belongs to the class, not to any instance
static field: one shared copy across all objects
static method: called without creating an object — ClassName.method()
main is static so JVM can call it without instantiating the class
